name.text: Estimating a power of a number near 2 or 3

questiontext.text:
By writing \({@Nd@}\) as \({@a@} + ({@dd@})\), use the first four terms of the expansion of \(({@a@} + x)^{@n@}\) to estimate \({@Nd@}^{@n@}\). Give your answer correct to 4 decimal places.

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Each term of \(({@a@} + x)^{@n@}\) is a row number times a power of \({@a@}\) times a power of \(x\): the powers of \({@a@}\) go down while the powers of \(x\) go up. Put \(x = {@dd@}\).

\(r\)Row number\({@a@}^{{@n@}-r}\)\(x^r\)Term
\({@rows[1][1]@}\)\({@rows[1][2]@}\)\({@rows[1][3]@}\)\({@rows[1][4]@}\)\({@rows[1][5]@}\)
\({@rows[2][1]@}\)\({@rows[2][2]@}\)\({@rows[2][3]@}\)\({@rows[2][4]@}\)\({@rows[2][5]@}\)
\({@rows[3][1]@}\)\({@rows[3][2]@}\)\({@rows[3][3]@}\)\({@rows[3][4]@}\)\({@rows[3][5]@}\)
\({@rows[4][1]@}\)\({@rows[4][2]@}\)\({@rows[4][3]@}\)\({@rows[4][4]@}\)\({@rows[4][5]@}\)

The sum of the four terms is \({@S4d@}\), so \({@Nd@}^{@n@} \approx {@R4@}\) to 4 decimal places. A calculator gives \({@calc@}\ldots\), which also rounds to \({@R4@}\).

questiondescription.text:
Binomial Expansions: approximating a power of a number near 2 or 3

Grade 12 CBE Core 1.2: Estimate (a + d)^n, a = 2 or 3, from the first four terms of (a + x)^n, to 4 decimal places.

Core

This question is adapted from Chapter 4, Section A, Exercise A, question 5 of Instone, S., Ling, J., Scruton, P., Shilton, S. and West, H., SMP AS/A2 Mathematics: Core 4 for AQA, Cambridge University Press, 2005: new numbers and powers, randomised, positive and negative d, with the estimate given to 4 decimal places.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text: Only your first term has a power of \({@a@}\). Each term also contains \({@a@}\) to a falling power: \({@a@}^{@n@}\), \({@a@}^{@n-1@}\), \({@a@}^{@n-2@}\), \({@a@}^{@n-3@}\).

node.description: Took out a^n, kept x = d

truefeedback.text: You took out \({@a@}^{@n@}\) but kept \(x = {@dd@}\). \({@a@} + ({@dd@}) = {@a@}\left(1 + \dfrac{ {@dd@} }{ {@a@} }\right)\), so inside the bracket \(x\) would be \(\dfrac{ {@dd@} }{ {@a@} }\). Easier: use \(({@a@} + x)^{@n@}\) with \(x = {@dd@}\).
That is only the first two terms; add the next two.

falsefeedback.text: The terms are \({@a@}^{@n@}\), \({@n@} \times {@a@}^{@n-1@} \times x\), \({@C2@} \times {@a@}^{@n-2@} \times x^2\) and \({@C3@} \times {@a@}^{@n-3@} \times x^3\), with \(x = {@dd@}\).
